title: Labor and the Workplace
summary: How US employment works: at-will hiring and firing, health insurance tied to jobs, where unions are strong, state-by-state minimum wages and the gig debate. Labor is often the largest cost line in a US case, and it explains why automation and offshoring pencil out.

blocks.title: At-will employment
blocks.body: Most US jobs are 'at will': employer or employee can end the relationship at any time, for any lawful reason, usually with no notice requirement. Limits come from anti-discrimination law, union contracts, individual contracts and some state rules; large layoffs can trigger federal WARN Act notice. Result: US firms adjust headcount faster than firms in many countries, and restructuring is a normal lever in cases.

blocks.title: Healthcare is tied to the job
items: Employer insurance covers ~154M people under 65 (KFF, 2025); it is a core part of a job offer.
Average family premium for employer coverage was ~$27K in 2025; employers pay most of it.
Benefits were ~30% of private-sector compensation cost in mid-2026 (BLS); wages ~70%.
Losing a job often means losing coverage, which reduces job mobility and raises the stakes of layoffs.
Part-time and contract workers often get fewer benefits, which is part of their cost appeal to employers.

rows: Labor contracts drive cost and plant decisions

blocks.title: Minimum wage varies by place
items: Federal minimum is $7.25 per hour, unchanged since 2009.
Many states and cities set much higher floors; Washington, California, Connecticut, New York and DC are above ~$16 in 2026.
Several Southern states have no state minimum and default to the federal rate.
Many states index their minimum to inflation, so floors rise automatically each year.
For restaurants and retail, the local wage floor can swing store-level economics sharply.

blocks.title: Gig work and contractor classification
blocks.body: Employees get minimum wage, overtime, unemployment insurance and employer payroll taxes; independent contractors do not. Gig platforms (ride-hailing, delivery) rely on contractor status, which is contested in courts and state legislatures, with California the best-known battleground. Independent contractors were ~7% of US employment in 2023 (BLS). Classification risk is a real cost scenario in any platform case.

blocks.title: India vs US: labor context
rows: High fully loaded cost; automation pays back faster
Formal-sector rules and approvals for larger firms
Largely separate from employment for most workers
Large pool of gig riders at low cost
Set by states with many categories
Federal floor plus higher state/city floors
Concentrated in public sector and some industries

blocks.title: Why automation and offshoring pencil out
items: Fully loaded labor cost (wages + benefits + payroll taxes) often runs well above the hourly wage.
Private-sector compensation averaged ~$47 per hour worked in June 2026 (BLS).
Labor shortages in warehousing, trucking and healthcare push firms to automate.
Offshoring back-office, IT and customer service to India and elsewhere has been common for decades.
Counterweights: tariffs, reshoring incentives, quality, time zones and public-image risk.

blocks.title: H-1B in brief
blocks.body: The H-1B visa lets US employers hire foreign professionals in specialty occupations. The annual cap is 65,000 plus 20,000 for US advanced-degree holders; universities and affiliated research nonprofits are exempt. Demand far exceeds supply, so a lottery is used, and since 2026 selection is weighted toward higher wage levels. A 2025 proclamation added a $100,000 payment for certain new petitions, which has been challenged in court.

blocks.title: Always fully load labor cost
blocks.body: When a case gives an hourly wage, add benefits and payroll taxes (BLS data imply roughly 1.4-1.5x wages for full-time private workers) before comparing against automation or outsourcing. Interviewers notice when you remember that a $20/hour worker costs the company much more than $20.

in_a_case: Warehouse automation: compare robot capex against fully loaded labor plus turnover and hiring costs; tight labor markets shorten payback.
Restaurant chain expansion: check state and city minimum wages; the same store format can be profitable in Texas and marginal in California.
Airline or automaker cost case: union contracts set wages and work rules; savings may require negotiation, not just a plan.
Delivery or gig platform: model a scenario where couriers are reclassified as employees and see what happens to unit economics.
Fit conversation: if asked about visas, be factual and calm; firms differ in sponsorship policies, so research each firm rather than assume.
